bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 11: Managing Linguistic Data
bib.venue: O'Reilly Media (book chapter; year inferred from the O'Reilly NLTK book, not printed in the chapter text)

question: How are annotated corpora structured, built, curated, converted between formats and described so that others can find and reuse them?
contributions: Uses TIMIT as a case study of corpus structure, then separates lexicon and text data types
Walks through the corpus life cycle: collection, annotation guidelines, quality control with inter-annotator agreement (kappa, windowdiff), curation versus evolution and standoff annotation
Shows how to convert and query XML and Toolbox data, and describes resources with Dublin Core and OLAC metadata

results.claim: Inter-annotator agreement should be reported, e.g. by double-annotating 10% of the corpus, and serves as an upper bound on the performance of any system trained on the corpus.
Agreement scores are task dependent: 90% agreement would be terrible for part-of-speech tagging but exceptional for semantic role labeling.
results.quote: 90% agreement would be a terrible score for part-of-speech

results.claim: Kappa corrects for chance: with four equally likely codes random annotators agree 25% of the time, which scores kappa = 0, and 50% agreement scores kappa = 0.333.
results.setup: Four equally likely labels, two annotators

results.claim: nltk.windowdiff with window size 3 gives 0 for s1 vs s1, 4 for s1 vs s2 and 16 for s2 vs s3 on three 23-character 0/1 boundary strings.
results.setup: Window size 3; strings of length 23 marking token boundaries
results.note: Toy strings; there is no benchmark.

results.claim: The Dublin Core consists of 15 metadata elements, each optional and repeatable.

limits: Corpus-engineering advice is general and not tested on any measured outcome; the only numbers are toy windowdiff strings, a kappa illustration and the Dublin Core element count.
Toolbox and XML sections are tooling tutorials tied to Python 2 and NLTK 2 APIs and to field linguistics; little carries to trained text pipelines.
Metadata standards (OLAC) are described but their adoption is not assessed.
Written before crowd-sourced and LLM-produced labels; says nothing about their agreement.
practices: Write annotation guidelines, annotate a sample twice and report agreement before training on a corpus (11.2).
Interpret agreement against task difficulty, and convert raw agreement to kappa to remove chance agreement (11.2).
Distribute annotations as standoff references to stable source identifiers so the source is not modified and independent annotations can be compared (11.2).
Give every released corpus a version and metadata record so others can find it (11.6).

terms.definition: the extent to which independent annotators assign the same labels to the same items
an agreement measure that corrects for the agreement expected by chance
a segmentation-agreement score from a sliding window that gives partial credit for near-miss boundaries
annotations stored apart from the source and referring to it by identifier
a set of 15 optional, repeatable metadata elements for resource discovery

lineage.note: Element set that OLAC metadata extends
Annotated speech corpus used as the structural case study
